displayQuote: I can't understand how anyone can write without rewriting everything over and over again

meta.title: Who really said "I can't understand how anyone can write without rewriting everything over and over again"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes, Tolstoy said it — in 1899, to his friend A. B. Goldenveizer. Printed in Talks with Tolstoi (Hogarth Press, 1923), p. 26, as "any one", not "anyone".
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I can't understand how anyone can write without rewriting everything over and over again'?
meta.ogDescription: Tolstoy really said it — at Yasnaya Polyana in 1899, recorded by A. B. Goldenveizer and printed in Talks with Tolstoi (Hogarth Press, 1923), page 26.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Recorded by the pianist A. B. Goldenveizer and printed in English as Talks with Tolstoi (Hogarth Press, 1923), page 26 — in an entry dated 2 August in the diary’s 1899 section, noting something Tolstoy had said the day before. The line is genuine, but it is secondhand and translated: a friend’s written-up record of a conversation, not a sentence Tolstoy published himself.

source.heading: Recorded at Yasnaya Polyana, 1899

source.excerpt: Yesterday L. N. spoke of the process of creative work: “I can’t understand how any one can write without rewriting everything over and over again. I scarcely ever re-read my published writings, but if by chance I come across a page, it always strikes me: All this must be rewritten; this is how I should have written it… I am always interested to trace the moment, which comes quite early, when the public is satisfied; and the artist thinks: They say it is good; but it is just at this point that the real work begins!”
trail: 1899, Yasnaya Polyana. Tolstoy makes the remark in conversation; Goldenveizer notes it the next day, in an entry dated 2 August, a page after describing the dense proof corrections for Resurrection — both passages are in the 1899 section ↗.
End of 1922, Moscow. Goldenveizer publishes volume 1 of his diary as Vblizi Tolstogo — his memories of a friendship of nearly fifteen years ↗.

1923, Richmond. S. S. Koteliansky and Virginia Woolf translate a selection; Leonard and Virginia Woolf publish it at the Hogarth Press as Talks with Tolstoi. The remark is on page 26 of the scanned first edition ↗.

1948 onward. Anthologies detach it from its source: Walter Allen’s Writers on Writing, a 1964 New York Times Book Review round-up, then Donald M. Murray’s 1968 writing textbook — the reprint chain traced by Quote Investigator ↗.
source.excerptNote: “L. N.” is Lev Nikolaevich — Tolstoy. Note the two-word “any one” of the 1923 translation, and the second half of the thought, which the popular one-line version drops.

author.name: Leo Tolstoy
author.kicker: The man who could not leave a page alone
author.heading: Leo Tolstoy
author.metaLine: 1828–1910 · Russian novelist, author of War and Peace and Anna Karenina
author.bio: Lev Nikolayevich Tolstoy wrote War and Peace (1869) and Anna Karenina (1878) before turning, in later life, to religious and moral writing that made Yasnaya Polyana a pilgrimage site for admirers, reformers and cranks alike. He was a notorious reviser — the friends and family who copied his drafts left repeated testimony to how many times a single passage could be redone. The remark about rewriting comes from that milieu: not from a published essay, but from an ordinary afternoon’s conversation that somebody happened to write down.

misattribution.heading: What gets garbled
misattribution.intro: No rival claimant here — nobody else is credited with this line. What goes wrong is how it travels.

items.why: It is almost always presented as something Tolstoy set down himself. He did not. It is a spoken remark, written up the next day by his friend A. B. Goldenveizer, and Quote Investigator flags precisely that indirectness in its verdict ↗.
The Koteliansky–Woolf translation reads “how any one can write” — two words. The one-word form now standard online is a later tidy-up; you can check the original spelling in the 1923 text ↗.

items.who: A Russian remark in English clothes
items.why: There is no ‘original’ English sentence to be faithful to. Every English version descends from the 1923 Hogarth Press rendering of Goldenveizer’s Russian, scanned here ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Tolstoy really said it, at Yasnaya Polyana in the summer of 1899. The sentence we quote is his friend’s record of it, published in Moscow in 1922 and in English in 1923 — and Quote Investigator calls that 1923 text (or the 1922 Russian) the most accurate version in circulation ↗.

context.heading: A summer spent rewriting
lead: An entry dated 31 July, just ahead of this one, finds Goldenveizer at Yasnaya Polyana working through the proofs of Resurrection. Tolstoy’s corrections were written so closely, he notes, that a magnifying glass was needed to read them, and a single printed proof-sheet could turn into three or four long pages copied out afresh — the same incident sometimes written dozens of times over ↗.

Resurrection appeared that same year, 1899 ↗. So the famous sentence about rewriting is not an aphorism composed at leisure; it is a man in the middle of the job saying out loud what the job feels like — and then adding the sting in the tail that most quotations leave off.
context.detailsSummary: The Hogarth Press connection, and how the line became workshop gospel
detailsBody: The English exists because of an unusual publishing pairing. Goldenveizer’s Russian diary came out in Moscow at the end of 1922; the following year S. S. Koteliansky and Virginia Woolf translated a selection of it, and Leonard and Virginia Woolf issued it from their own Hogarth Press in Richmond ↗. Every English version of the quotation in circulation descends from that book.

From there it moved into the literature of craft. Quote Investigator follows it into Walter Allen’s 1948 compendium Writers on Writing, a 1964 New York Times Book Review feature called “Treasure Chest,” and Donald M. Murray’s 1968 A Writer Teaches Writing — the chain of reprints is set out there ↗. Anthologising is what stripped the source off it.
